input: Map out a realistic debt payoff snowball plan

keyUnknowns.whyItMatters: The number and types of debts (credit cards, student loans, car loans, medical bills, etc.) determines the complexity of the snowball sequence and whether any debts should be excluded or treated specially.
The total monthly amount available for debt repayment is the single biggest driver of how aggressive or realistic the plan can be and directly sets the payoff timeline.
Whether income is stable or variable (e.g. freelance, seasonal) changes how much buffer to build in and whether a fixed monthly payment plan is feasible.
If a partner or household member shares the debt or income, the plan must account for joint obligations and combined cash flow rather than just one person's finances.
Some people want to stay strictly orthodox (smallest balance first, always) while others want flexibility to pause or redirect funds for emergencies — this shapes the rules built into the plan.
Knowing the target end-state — a specific debt-free date, a motivational milestone, or just 'as fast as possible' — determines how the plan measures progress and declares success.
The format needed (spreadsheet, written schedule, app-ready breakdown, etc.) and where the user will track it affects how the plan should be structured and handed off.

gold.taskTitle: Map out a realistic debt payoff snowball plan
gold.taskDescription: Build a structured, step-by-step debt snowball plan that prioritises debts from smallest to largest balance and applies freed-up payments progressively until all debts are cleared.

questions.title: How many debts do you have, and what types are they?
questions.description: Identify the full list of debts to be included in the snowball — e.g. credit cards, car loan, student loan, medical bill — so the correct payoff order and sequence can be built.

questions.title: How much extra money can you put toward debt each month?
questions.description: Determine the total monthly surplus available beyond minimum payments, as this is the core engine of the snowball and sets the realistic pace of the plan.

questions.title: Is your monthly income stable or does it vary?
questions.description: Understand income predictability to decide whether the plan uses a fixed monthly snowball amount or needs a tiered/flexible structure for low-income months.

questions.title: Are you planning this alone or with a partner?
questions.description: Clarify whether this is a solo plan or a household plan, since shared debts and combined income require coordinating two people's cash flows and commitments.

questions.title: Should the plan pause the snowball if an emergency comes up?
questions.description: Establish the rule set for the plan — strict snowball-only, or with built-in decision points to pause and redirect funds — so it matches how the user actually wants to operate.

questions.title: Do you have a target debt-free date in mind?
questions.description: Identify whether the plan should be reverse-engineered from a deadline, optimised for maximum speed, or structured around a motivational milestone like clearing one card first.

questions.title: What format do you want the finished plan delivered in?
questions.description: Determine the output format — spreadsheet, month-by-month written schedule, a simple list, or something app-ready — so the plan is immediately usable without extra reformatting.
